presentingComplaint: Six weeks of drenching night sweats, low-grade evening fevers and unintentional weight loss in a frail, community-dwelling elderly man.
history: A 79-year-old retired schoolteacher, living alone and increasingly frail over the past year (slower gait, two falls, needs help with shopping), presents with about six weeks of insidious symptoms. He reports soaking through his bedclothes with sweat most nights, needing to change them, and feeling feverish in the evenings although he has not measured his temperature. He has lost roughly 8 kg (from 68 to 60 kg) without dieting and his appetite is poor. He notices painless lumps in the left side of his neck and left armpit that have slowly enlarged. He is profoundly fatigued and now spends most of the day in a chair. No cough, haemoptysis, dysuria, diarrhoea or localising symptoms. He is a lifelong non-smoker, drinks minimally, and has no known TB contact, no recent travel, and no rural or animal exposure. Past history: hypertension, osteoarthritis, cataract surgery. Medications: amlodipine, occasional paracetamol. He has had no antibiotics and no hospitalisation in the past year. His GP treated him empirically for a presumed chest infection two weeks ago with no improvement.
examination: Frail, cachectic elderly man appearing older than his stated age, alert and oriented, not acutely toxic. Multiple firm, rubbery, non-tender, matted lymph nodes in the left cervical chain (largest ~3 cm) and a 2.5 cm left axillary node. Spleen palpable 3 cm below the costal margin; liver edge just palpable, non-tender. Mild conjunctival pallor. No jaundice, no rash, no joint swelling. Chest clear, no focal consolidation. Abdomen soft, no other mass. No focal neurology. No peripheral oedema.

labs.peripheral_smear: no blasts; mild rouleaux; no schistocytes

imaging: Chest radiograph clear, no consolidation or cavitation. Contrast CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis: enlarged left cervical, supraclavicular, axillary and para-aortic lymph nodes (multiple >1.5 cm), and splenomegaly (16 cm) without focal splenic lesions. No lung mass or cavity. No hepatic abscess. No sanctuary of pus or focal infective collection.
microbiology: Blood cultures x2 no growth at 5 days. Urinalysis unremarkable. Two sputum samples negative on smear; CBNAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF) on sputum not detected. HIV serology negative. Malaria smear/RDT negative. No infective focus identified after systematic screen.
differentialDiagnoses: Lymphoma / occult malignancy with B-symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, evening fever, generalised lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, high LDH and ESR)
Disseminated tuberculosis (constitutional symptoms, splenomegaly, high ESR) - excluded on smear/CBNAAT and clear chest imaging
Pyrexia of unknown origin from an undiagnosed infective/inflammatory cause
Acute leukaemia (marrow-based) - smear shows no blasts
Multiple myeloma (elderly, anaemia, high ESR) - no CRAB/lytic lesions or paraprotein evident
finalDiagnosis: Underlying malignancy presenting with classical B-symptoms (constitutional syndrome) - generalised lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, anaemia of malignancy and markedly elevated LDH/beta-2-microglobulin, most consistent with lymphoma; requires tissue diagnosis by excisional lymph node biopsy.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Enlargement of Lymph Nodes and Spleen
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Approach to the Patient with Cancer
NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines - B-cell Lymphomas - 2024
British Society for Haematology - Investigation and Management of Lymphadenopathy - 2023
stewardship: Not applicable - non-infective presentation. Empirical antibiotics are not indicated; the constitutional syndrome reflects underlying malignancy, and the priority is expedited tissue diagnosis rather than antimicrobial therapy.
contraindications: Avoid empirical antitubercular therapy before tissue/microbiological confirmation - masks and delays a lymphoma diagnosis
Avoid corticosteroids before excisional biopsy - can lyse lymphoma tissue and render histology non-diagnostic
Avoid fine-needle aspiration alone for suspected lymphoma - inadequate for architectural subtyping; excisional biopsy preferred
edgeCases: In a frail elderly patient B-symptoms are easily mis-attributed to ageing, depression or occult infection, delaying oncological workup
Disseminated TB is the key mimic in the Indian setting and must be actively excluded, but negative CBNAAT plus clear chest imaging and matted painless nodes favour malignancy
High uric acid and LDH raise concern for spontaneous tumour lysis in high-grade lymphoma - monitor renal function and electrolytes
expectedMaiK: Recognise the constitutional B-symptom syndrome (weight loss + drenching night sweats + evening fever) with generalised lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly as a red-flag for underlying malignancy, and prioritise excisional lymph node biopsy for tissue diagnosis rather than empirical anti-infective therapy.
expectedNextQuestions: Duration and pattern of the fever, and quantity of weight lost over what period?
Are the enlarged nodes painful, and do they hurt after alcohol?
Any pruritus, bone pain, easy bruising or bleeding?
Any TB contact, travel, or animal/rural exposure to exclude infective mimics?
Any prior malignancy, B-symptom-provoking medications, or HIV risk factors?
expectedInvestigations: Excisional lymph node biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry
Full blood count with peripheral smear, LDH, uric acid, beta-2-microglobulin
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
HIV serology, and TB screen (sputum CBNAAT) to exclude the disseminated-TB mimic
regressionAssertions: Engine should surface malignancy_b as the leading diagnosis given B-symptoms plus generalised lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly
DISSEMINATED_TB must appear in the differential but be down-ranked by negative CBNAAT and clear chest imaging
No empirical antibiotics should be recommended (infective:false; stewardship tier null)
Excisional lymph node biopsy should be the top recommended investigation for tissue diagnosis
